chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
Capstone Energy+ emerged from a compressed but consequential corporate metamorphosis. Founded in 1988 in Van Nuys, California as Capstone Turbine Corporation, the company spent three decades commercialising the microturbine before renaming itself Capstone Green Energy Holdings in 2021 to signal a pivot toward integrated microgrid contracting. That pivot proved insufficient to arrest a liquidity spiral: on September 28, 2023, Capstone Green Energy filed for Chapter 11 in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware in a pre-packaged restructuring, with Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group as the dominant pre-petition creditor. The company emerged on December 7, 2023 with a restructured balance sheet and new ownership. On May 15, 2026 — eight days before this dossier's snapshot date — the company completed its final identity shift, legally renaming itself Capstone Energy+, Inc. Its OTCQX ticker, CGEH, remained unchanged. The OTCQX listing reflects the reduced disclosure cadence appropriate to a post-emergence entity: public filings arrive materially less frequently than those of a NASDAQ-listed peer, and disclosure gaps are noted throughout this dossier where they constrain analysis.

## Core Business

Capstone designs, manufactures, and services microturbine systems spanning 30 kilowatts (C30) through 1.2 megawatts (C1200S), with packaged multi-unit configurations reaching several megawatts of on-site generating capacity. The machines burn natural gas, biogas, propane, and flare gas with lower NOx emissions than reciprocating engine alternatives and no oil-lubricated components, yielding lower service intervals. Post-emergence strategy has emphasised Energy-as-a-Service: power purchase agreements, energy service agreements, and long-term equipment rentals that convert capital-equipment sales into multi-year contracted revenue. In fiscal 2025, the rental and EaaS segment contributed $14.4 million — 17 percent of total revenue — establishing a recurring baseline that did not exist at the same scale before the restructuring. [FY2025 Press Release](https://www.capstoneenergyplus.com/news/press-releases/detail/4040/)

Customer applications span oil and gas flare-gas utilisation at upstream well sites (the largest single application category), industrial combined heat and power for food and agricultural manufacturing, district energy for university campuses and hospital complexes, hospitality cogeneration, and — emerging — AI data centre backup and bridge power. The company had deployed more than 10,600 units across 88 countries as of the May 2026 rebrand announcement.

## Revenue and Financial Posture

Pre-Chapter-11 revenue stood at approximately $77 million in fiscal 2023 (ended March 31, 2023). The restructuring year — fiscal 2024 — produced $91.2 million as order activity pulled forward ahead of the filing. Fiscal 2025 revenue declined to $85.6 million, partly on European market hesitancy during the post-emergence transition, but the year produced Capstone's first-ever positive full-year adjusted EBITDA of $7.9 million. In the nine months ended December 31, 2025, revenue reached $83.0 million, up 42 percent year-over-year, with trailing twelve-month revenue of approximately $110 million. [Q3 FY2026 Results](https://ir.capstoneenergyplus.com/press-releases/detail/4064)

| Period | Revenue | Adj. EBITDA |
|---|---|---|
| FY2023 (pre-filing) | ~$77M | n/a |
| FY2024 (emergence year) | $91.2M | n/a |
| FY2025 | $85.6M | +$7.9M |
| TTM through Dec 2025 | ~$110M | — |

Cash at March 31, 2025 stood at $8.7 million against total liabilities of $82.6 million, producing a stockholders' deficiency of $21.6 million — a balance sheet consistent with a company still digesting its emergence. That posture shifted materially when Monarch Alternative Capital closed a $112.5 million strategic investment on March 31, 2026: $80 million in senior convertible preferred stock, $15 million in common equity, and a $17.5 million concurrent PIPE. Proceeds fully redeemed Goldman Sachs's legacy preferred position, extinguishing the dominant structural liability of the post-emergence balance sheet. [Monarch Investment Close](https://ir.capstoneenergyplus.com/press-releases/detail/4066) Post-Monarch balance sheet data was not yet public within the snapshot window; Q4 FY2026 earnings were scheduled for June 25, 2026.

## Leadership and Market Position

Vincent J. Canino was appointed President and CEO on March 11, 2024, three months after emergence, succeeding Robert Flexon who held the interim role through the restructuring. Canino brought thirty years of energy-sector experience including the chief operating officer role at long-duration storage company ESS Tech (NYSE: GWH) and the president and CEO role at Smardt Chiller Group. John P. Miller assumed the Interim CFO role in November 2025. As of May 22, 2026, CGEH traded at approximately $10.02 per share, implying a market capitalisation of roughly $304 million on approximately 30.3 million shares outstanding — a 52-week range of $0.31 to $13.80 that captures the full arc of the post-restructuring equity discovery process. [StockAnalysis](https://stockanalysis.com/quote/otc/CGEH/)

The AI data centre narrative, while prominent in post-emergence investor communications, remained at the framework stage within the snapshot window. A memorandum of understanding with Microgrids 4 AI (MG4AI) in September 2025 and an 800-volt direct-current microturbine architecture announcement in October 2025 established the technology positioning; no revenue-generating customer contracts had been publicly disclosed as of May 23, 2026. [MG4AI MOU](https://www.capstoneenergyplus.com/news/press-releases/detail/4048/)

## The Central Question

Capstone Energy+ enters its post-restructuring growth phase with a cleaner balance sheet following the Monarch transaction, a revenue trajectory approaching $110 million on a trailing basis, and a commitment — as part of the Monarch terms — to pursue a national exchange listing within twelve months of the March 2026 close. The dossier asks the harder questions: what does the restructured cap table actually deliver to equity holders once Monarch's convertible preferred is layered in, how durable is the EaaS revenue conversion against Bloom Energy, Cummins, Caterpillar, and distributed gas-generation alternatives, and what does AI data centre bridge-power demand require that Capstone's microturbine architecture can credibly supply at commercial scale?

chapters.title: From 1988 Capstone Turbine through Green Energy rebrand to Chapter 11 and Energy+
chapters.body:
## Origins: The 1988 Founding and the Promise of Distributed Generation

Capstone Turbine Corporation spent the 1990s refining its air-bearing microturbine technology, accumulating intellectual property, and cultivating early adopters in oil-and-gas and industrial cogeneration segments. The C30 — a 30-kilowatt unit — was its initial commercial offering. By the late 1990s, the company had working hardware, a growing installed base, and enough commercial traction to attract capital-market interest.

## The 2000 NASDAQ Listing and the Accumulating Deficit

Capstone Turbine Corporation went public on NASDAQ in 2000, raising capital in a market simultaneously beginning to price in a very different kind of future. The listing positioned Capstone as a clean-energy technology company at the intersection of distributed generation and low-emissions power — a story that resonated with the emerging green technology narrative even before "ESG" had become standard institutional vocabulary.

What followed was a multi-decade exercise in sustaining a commercially viable product against a backdrop of chronic operating losses. Fiscal year after fiscal year, Capstone reported revenues that demonstrated genuine market demand — customers in oil and gas, industrial cogeneration, district energy, hotel combined heat and power, and related segments were buying and deploying microturbines — while also reporting operating losses that accumulated into a nine-figure cumulative deficit. The microturbine technology worked. The business model did not close.

Revenue fluctuated within a comparatively narrow band — $73 million to $95 million across fiscal years 2020 through 2023 — without translating into sustained profitability. (See Snapshot for detailed revenue table.) The underlying challenge was structural: microturbines occupy a specific niche in distributed power, competing with reciprocating gas generators on emissions and fuel flexibility but carrying higher upfront capital costs that demand longer payback periods. Converting that niche appeal into the scale required to absorb a public company's sales infrastructure, product development overhead, and service organisation proved persistently difficult. By the early 2020s, the company had spent more than two decades publicly listed on NASDAQ without demonstrating a durable pathway to positive operating income. Accumulated deficit disclosures in the company's SEC filings had grown to exceed $1 billion.

Yet the product line had continued to mature in parallel. The C30 had been joined by C65, C200S, C600S, C800S, and C1000S signature-series configurations, and eventually by the C1200S at 1.2 megawatts — enabling packaged multi-unit microgrid systems capable of delivering several megawatts of dispatchable power from a single coordinated installation. The technology was not stagnant; the commercial model was the constraint.

## 2021: Capstone Green Energy and the EaaS Pivot

Against a backdrop of accelerating ESG capital allocation and growing institutional interest in energy-transition narratives, management executed the company's first corporate rename in 2021. Capstone Turbine Corporation became Capstone Green Energy Corporation — a rebranding positioned not merely as a marketing exercise but as a signal of strategic direction.

The pivot was toward Energy-as-a-Service. Rather than selling microturbine hardware and collecting a product margin, the company would structure integrated microgrid contracts under which customers paid a recurring service fee in exchange for on-site dispatchable power, heat recovery, and ongoing asset management — with Capstone owning or co-financing the underlying equipment. The EaaS model promised more predictable recurring revenue, deeper long-term customer relationships, and a valuation framework more consistent with infrastructure-service multiples than conventional industrial equipment sales.

The rationale was coherent. The execution challenge was financing. Converting a capital-light hardware-sale model into a capital-intensive equipment-ownership model requires balance-sheet capacity that Capstone Green Energy did not possess in abundance. Service contract origination demands working capital to deploy assets ahead of recurring revenue recognition. For a company carrying a persistent operating deficit and constrained access to investment-grade debt markets, the EaaS transition demanded bridge financing that would prove increasingly difficult to sustain as the macro environment shifted.

## September 28, 2023: Chapter 11 in the District of Delaware

On September 28, 2023, Capstone Green Energy Holdings, Inc. filed for Chapter 11 protection in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware. The filing had been structured in advance as a prepackaged plan — the company had negotiated the terms of its restructuring with its principal secured creditor, Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group, before appearing in court, with the specific intention of confirming a reorganisation plan and emerging from Chapter 11 on a compressed timeline.

The precipitating factors, as reflected in court filings and contemporaneous public disclosure, included liquidity tightening across a rising-rate macroeconomic environment that had compressed working capital availability across leveraged industrial businesses, customer-receivable concerns that created cash-conversion stress, and the operational scaling challenges inherent in pivoting an asset-light hardware business toward an equipment-ownership EaaS model. The pre-petition balance sheet carried secured debt obligations to Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending that the company could not service on an ongoing basis.

Long-tenured chief executive Darren Jamison, who had led the company through the 2021 Green Energy rebrand and the EaaS strategic pivot, departed as the restructuring process unfolded. The prepackaged structure itself reflected the relative concentration of the creditor group: Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending held the dominant secured position, enabling bilateral negotiation of plan terms before the court filing rather than the protracted multi-party negotiations that characterise contested Chapter 11 proceedings. A prepackaged confirmation compresses the bankruptcy timeline dramatically, reducing the value destruction — customer attrition, management distraction, vendor credit tightening — that accumulates during extended court-supervised reorganisations.

## December 7, 2023: Emergence and the Capstone Energy+ Rebrand

Capstone Green Energy emerged from Chapter 11 on December 7, 2023 — approximately ten weeks after the filing date, a compressed timeline consistent with the prepackaged structure's design. The emergence was the product of a confirmed plan of reorganisation that converted the secured debt held by Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group and other pre-petition creditors into reorganised equity in the restructured entity. Pre-Chapter-11 common shareholders — holders of the NASDAQ-listed equity — were substantially wiped out, consistent with the standard priority waterfall in a prepackaged restructuring where secured creditor claims exceeded enterprise value available to junior interests.

The post-emergence company — now trading on OTCQX under the ticker CGEH, a material step down in listing tier from its NASDAQ predecessor — subsequently rebranded as Capstone Energy+, Inc. The name change shed the "Green Energy" framing that had defined the 2021-to-2023 chapter and adopted a posture more explicitly oriented toward reliable, dispatchable power delivery. Post-emergence financial disclosure cadence reflects the OTCQX reporting standard, materially less granular than the SEC-reporting cadence of the NASDAQ predecessor; investors should treat post-emergence financial detail as a disclosure gap relative to what the pre-Chapter-11 entity provided through quarterly 10-Q and annual 10-K filings.

The shift in positioning was not incidental. By late 2023 and into 2024, the data centre infrastructure build-out driven by generative AI workloads had begun producing visible, documented pressure on utility interconnection queues across major US markets. Hyperscale operators and the project developers serving them faced multi-year waits for grid interconnect capacity at a moment when their power demand timelines were measured in months. On-site dispatchable generation — gas-fired units capable of bridging the gap between construction completion and permanent grid connection — was emerging as an active procurement category.

Capstone Energy+'s microturbine product line was, by this point, a 35-year-old technology with a documented field record across oil and gas, industrial cogeneration, and district energy. Its post-emergence strategic communications began positioning that record explicitly against the data centre bridge-power opportunity.

---

What the long arc of Capstone's corporate history produced, as of the December 2023 emergence, was this: a mature, field-proven distributed power technology developed across more than three decades; a public-company tenure characterised by genuine commercial adoption in multiple end markets but unbroken operating losses that accumulated past $1 billion; two corporate renames reflecting successive strategic pivots — from turbine hardware manufacturer to green-energy service integrator to dispatchable-power infrastructure provider; and a restructured equity now held by former creditors, trading on OTCQX rather than NASDAQ, at a company a fraction of the size its NASDAQ-era overhead implied. The company that filed in Delaware in September 2023 was not a failed technology. It was a proven technology that had never resolved the commercial tension between niche-market demand and the cost structure of a listed industrial enterprise. Whether Capstone Energy+ can resolve that tension under its post-emergence structure, in a market newly animated by AI data centre power demand, is the central question this dossier addresses.

chapters.title: Microturbine product lines, EaaS contracting, and customer applications
chapters.body:
## Product Architecture

Capstone's product catalogue spans six nameplate configurations from 30 kilowatts to 1.2 megawatts, all sharing the air-bearing design that eliminates liquid lubrication and reduces scheduled maintenance intervals.

The entry-level C30 delivers 30 kilowatts and was, for much of the company's early history, the unit through which Capstone established its reference base in niche applications — remote power, oil-field instrumentation, early CHP trials. The C65 (65 kW) occupied a similar niche applications tier. Both units were rendered commercially marginal in later years as the economics of scale pushed customers toward larger configurations; the C30 and C65 appear largely as legacy product in post-emergence communications, though they remain catalogued.

The practical workhorse of the fleet is the C200S, a 200-kilowatt unit whose modular footprint made it the basis for Capstone's packaged multi-turbine systems. The Signature Series — designated C600S, C800S, and C1000S — are factory-integrated packages combining three, four, or five C200S modules within a common enclosure with shared power electronics, control architecture, and heat recovery hardware. The C1000S delivers one megawatt from a configuration roughly twenty feet in length, a factor that matters materially at constrained urban and industrial sites. The C1200S, rated at 1.2 megawatts, represents the top of the single-enclosure product line and was introduced to compete more directly with small gas turbines and large reciprocating generator sets in the 750 kW–1.5 MW range. Packaged microgrid systems combining multiple C1000S or C1200S units with inverter hardware, battery storage, and supervisory control software extend the addressable capacity to several megawatts at a single site.

## Technology Characteristics

Key differentiators against reciprocating engines: (1) Maintenance intervals measured in 8,000 hours versus 500–2,000 for gensets — most valuable in remote applications. (2) NOx emissions below 9 ppm (some configurations below 5 ppm) without SCR aftertreatment — opening market access in air-quality-sensitive jurisdictions like California's SCAQMD. (3) Fuel flexibility across pipeline natural gas, associated gas, biogas, landfill gas, and hydrogen blends. (4) Electrical efficiency of ~33 percent at C200S full load; with heat recovery, system efficiency reaches 70–80 percent.

## The EaaS contracting model

Capstone's Energy-as-a-Service offering, developed progressively during the final years before the Chapter 11 filing and carried forward as a stated priority under the post-emergence management structure, restructures the traditional capital-sale transaction into a long-term service contract. Under the EaaS model, Capstone or an authorised distributor installs, owns, and operates the microturbine system at a customer's facility. The customer pays for delivered energy — kilowatt-hours of electricity and, where applicable, thermal output — under a multi-year agreement, typically structured over seven to fifteen years, rather than purchasing the equipment outright.

The strategic logic for Capstone is straightforward: EaaS converts a lumpy, project-dependent equipment revenue stream into contracted recurring service revenue, smoothing cash flow and, in principle, supporting a more predictable financial profile. For customers — particularly in the industrial and commercial segments where capital allocation committees scrutinise balance sheet additions — the model reduces the up-front barrier to adoption and transfers technology and maintenance risk back to the vendor.

Segment-level disclosure of EaaS contract value, backlog, or revenue contribution as a distinct line item has been limited in Capstone's OTCQX filings through the period covered by this dossier. The company has disclosed EaaS as a strategic priority and cited customer wins in IR communications, but the absence of the detailed segment reporting required of NASDAQ- or NYSE-listed companies means that external assessment of the EaaS revenue conversion trajectory is constrained by the disclosure environment. Investors relying solely on public filings encounter a material information gap on this dimension.

## Oil and gas: the core installed base

The oil and gas vertical has historically represented Capstone's largest and most durable customer segment. The core application is associated gas utilisation at upstream well sites: natural gas produced co-mingled with crude oil that, in the absence of pipeline takeaway infrastructure or economic incentive to process, operators would otherwise flare or vent. Installing a Capstone microturbine at a well pad converts that gas stream into on-site electricity — powering pumps, compression, instrumentation, and worker accommodation — without requiring a utility grid connection. The economics are governed by the spread between the cost of flaring (regulatory, reputational, and operational) and the value of the electricity displaced; in active shale basins with active flaring-reduction regulation, that spread has supported robust demand for the product.

Midstream applications extend the footprint: compression stations, gas processing facilities, and pipeline measurement stations have deployed Capstone units where the combination of fuel availability, remote location, and emissions compliance requirements makes reciprocating alternatives less attractive. Drilling rig power, where the rig itself generates electricity for its own operations from wellhead gas, represents a more episodic but recurring application.

The oil and gas segment is also where Capstone's fuel flexibility is most commercially valuable. Associated gas composition varies widely by basin and by well; the turbine's tolerance for fuel variability reduces the conditioning requirement and lowers the total installed cost relative to reciprocating competitors that require tighter fuel specifications.

## Industrial cogeneration, district energy, and hospitality

Industrial CHP has been the second major customer category throughout Capstone's commercial history. The application is straightforward: a C200S or Signature Series unit provides base-load or near-base-load power generation at a manufacturing or processing facility, while exhaust heat is recovered for steam, hot water, or direct process heating. Food and beverage processing, pharmaceuticals, and light manufacturing have all appeared in the company's reference case library. The economics are most compelling where the facility operates continuously, has a stable thermal load, and faces high grid electricity tariffs with significant demand charge components.

University campuses, hospital complexes, and district energy schemes represent a related but distinct sub-segment. These customers typically require high-reliability baseload generation, often have both heating and cooling loads amenable to absorption chilling from exhaust heat, and operate under sustainability mandates that favour lower-emissions distributed generation. Hospitality — hotels and resorts with continuous hot water, heating, and power requirements — follows similar logic.

## The emerging AI data centre opportunity

The post-emergence strategic communications from Capstone Energy+ placed notable emphasis on AI data centre backup and bridge power as an incremental customer category. The thesis tracks a well-documented infrastructure constraint: hyperscale data centre operators pursuing gigawatt-scale capacity expansions in the 2023–2026 period encountered utility interconnect queues extending to three, four, or more years at preferred sites across the United States. Operators under competitive pressure to bring AI training and inference capacity online could not wait for grid connections. Dispatchable on-site generation — gas-fired, low-emissions, capable of meeting air quality permit requirements in constrained jurisdictions — represented one technical pathway.

Capstone's Signature Series and packaged multi-megawatt systems are positioned, in the company's framing, to serve this need: multi-MW configurations assembled from C1000S or C1200S modules, fuelled by pipeline natural gas, capable of operating in island mode without grid synchronisation, and meeting air quality thresholds that would disqualify diesel backup generator arrays in markets like California. The low-maintenance air-bearing architecture reduces operating burden during potentially multi-year pre-interconnect operating periods.

What the public record through the May 2026 snapshot date does not fully establish is the extent to which this positioning translated into signed contracts, awarded projects, or recognised revenue from the hyperscale or co-location data centre segment. OTCQX disclosure discipline does not require the customer-level or segment-level transparency that would allow external investors to size the contribution. The AI data centre narrative is coherent and structurally plausible; its financial materialisation, as of the frozen window, remains incompletely evidenced in Capstone Energy+'s public filings.

chapters.title: Pre-Chapter-11 trajectory, post-emergence cap table, and the EaaS conversion path
chapters.body:
## A Revenue Band That Never Translated Into Cash

For most of Capstone Turbine's two-decade run as a public company, the financial narrative followed a pattern sophisticated investors in small-cap industrial technology would recognise immediately: credible product, real customers, recurring revenue that never converted to operating profitability. The four fiscal years immediately preceding the September 2023 Chapter 11 filing traced a revenue band between roughly $73 million and $95 million — wide enough to suggest a functioning business, narrow enough to signal that scale was not happening.

What those revenue numbers did not show was a path to cash generation. (Pre-Chapter-11 revenue ranged from $73 million to $95 million across FY2020–FY2023; see Snapshot for detailed table.) Capstone had carried operating losses throughout its public-company tenure stretching back to its 2000 listing — a structural feature of microturbine economics that the company's own disclosures repeatedly flagged as a going-concern risk. The underlying technology was not experimental; the C65, C200S, and C1000S product families had logged cumulative installed-hours across oil and gas, cogeneration, and district energy applications over years. The problem was not technical immaturity. It was that the capital structure of an equipment manufacturer selling into project-finance-sensitive energy markets left persistent working capital tension between order intake, production expenditure, and customer-payment cycles.

**Note on operating loss magnitude:** Specific quarterly and annual operating loss figures for each fiscal year through FY2023 are derivable from Capstone Green Energy's NASDAQ-era 10-K and 10-Q filings via SEC EDGAR; those filings constitute the primary source for precise loss quantum and gross margin trajectory. The prep data for this dossier does not reproduce those line items, and the dossier declines to estimate them.

## What Broke in 2023

The September 28, 2023 Chapter 11 filing in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware was the formal acknowledgment of a liquidity crisis that had been building through a combination of pressures. Capstone's post-filing disclosures and the bankruptcy court record identified several converging factors: tightened liquidity, customer receivable concerns, and broader operational scaling challenges. The oil and gas segment — a meaningful portion of Capstone's project base, particularly associated-gas utilisation at upstream well sites — had historically involved project customers whose own cash cycles were sensitive to commodity price movement. When receivable collection slowed, a company with Capstone's operating loss structure had limited buffer to absorb the lag.

The prepackaged Chapter 11 structure (detailed in Corporate History) compressed the in-court timeline to roughly ten weeks. Pre-Chapter-11 common stockholders received substantially wiped-out treatment, consistent with standard absolute priority enforcement when senior secured claims exceeded recoverable enterprise value.

**Disclosure gap:** The precise post-emergence ownership table — percentage holdings of Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending versus other creditor groups, any management equity incentive pool, any retained stub equity for legacy holders — has not been reproduced in detail in the OTCQX-cadence disclosures available as of the May 2026 snapshot date. The OTCQX market imposes materially lower public reporting obligations than the NASDAQ listing Capstone held pre-bankruptcy, and the company's post-emergence filings reflect that reduced cadence. Investors requiring a precise cap table should engage directly with Capstone Energy+ investor relations.

## The OTCQX Entity: What Post-Emergence Disclosure Confirms and What It Does Not

The OTCQX listing imposes a materially lighter disclosure regime than Capstone's prior NASDAQ status, with no quarterly 10-Q cadence or 8-K current-reporting obligations — a structural gap noted throughout this dossier.

Post-emergence revenue trajectory and cash position as of the May 2026 snapshot are areas where this dossier explicitly defers to direct verification via current Capstone Energy+ IR communications and any OTCQX-filed annual report for the fiscal period ending March 2025 or March 2026. The prep data confirms the company's post-emergence strategic refocus and the AI data centre positioning but does not reproduce audited post-emergence financials. Any investor model built on assumptions about post-emergence revenue or balance sheet cash should treat those figures as requiring primary verification.

## The EaaS Conversion: Economics and Strategic Rationale

The EaaS model's appeal to a post-restructuring equity base is straightforward: converting lumpy equipment-sale revenue into recurring multi-year service contracts. The FY2022-to-FY2023 revenue compression from $95 million to $77 million illustrates the volatility inherent in project-sale timing that EaaS seeks to smooth.

The credit implications of this transition are non-trivial. EaaS projects require upfront capital to procure and install generation assets before recurring revenue begins accruing. For a post-restructuring entity with a reorganised balance sheet and constrained access to capital markets, the pace at which EaaS deployment can be funded — whether through the company's own balance sheet, project finance structures, or third-party energy financing partners — directly governs how quickly the recurring revenue base can grow. Capstone Energy+'s ability to originate EaaS projects at scale will be a function of its post-emergence financial capacity as much as its commercial origination capability, and the current disclosure record does not permit a precise assessment of either constraint.

**Disclosure gap:** The current EaaS versus equipment-sale revenue mix, backlog composition, and contracted EaaS megawatts or project count as of the May 2026 snapshot are not detailed in the available prep data. Investors should query Capstone Energy+ IR directly for current pipeline and backlog disclosure.

## The Structural Inheritance

What Capstone Energy+ carried out of bankruptcy was a technology platform with a multi-decade commercial track record — microturbines operating in oil fields, hospitals, university campuses, and cogeneration applications across multiple continents — a restructured balance sheet that eliminated the senior debt burden that had contributed to the liquidity crisis, and a reorganised equity base whose return expectations were priced to the post-emergence entry point rather than the pre-bankruptcy capital structure. That combination is the starting point from which any assessment of the EaaS conversion path and the AI data centre opportunity must be constructed.

The persistent challenge is that Capstone has been, for its entire public-company life, a business that required more capital than its operating cash flows generated. The question the post-emergence equity base must answer is whether the EaaS revenue model, applied to an AI data centre market that did not exist as a meaningful revenue category during Capstone's NASDAQ years, changes that equation — or whether the structural inheritance is more durable than the rebranding suggests.

chapters.title: Pre-Chapter-11 quarters through emergence and post-emergence trajectory
chapters.body:
## A Long Ascent Interrupted

Fiscal year 2022's $95 million revenue — a high-water mark — coincided with rapid EaaS rental fleet expansion: the fleet under contract had grown 126 percent year-over-year to 40 megawatts by Q3 FY2023. Then the wheels came off.

## The Quarters Before the Fall

Quarterly results in fiscal year 2023 told a story of operational fragility behind the revenue headline. First-quarter revenue of $18.7 million was 16 percent above the year-ago period; the second quarter at $20.8 million added a further 21 percent gain. But the third quarter, covering October through December 2022, slipped to $19.6 million, down five percent year-on-year, as supply-chain disruptions, elevated freight costs, and component shortages compressed product shipments. Gross margin for that nine-month stretch clocked 16 percent — well below the 25-percent target management had consistently described to investors.

Darren Jamison, who had served as president and chief executive since 2006 — a 16-year tenure that spanned the original Capstone Turbine identity, the 2021 rebranding to Capstone Green Energy, and the entire EaaS pivot — acknowledged the pressure directly. "Although product shipments during the third quarter were challenged as we continue to battle supply chain disruptions and higher costs," Jamison said in the Q3 fiscal-2023 earnings release, "I expect this will begin to be offset by our price increases implemented at the end of January." He described EaaS as "a pivotal factor in achieving this goal." The full-year fiscal-2023 result came in at approximately $77 million — a drop of roughly $18 million from the fiscal-2022 peak.

Those headwinds also masked a deteriorating balance sheet. Pre-petition debt and accrued interest stood at $56.0 million, principally owed under an amended and restated note purchase agreement dated October 1, 2020, with Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group, L.P. as collateral agent and its affiliate Broad Street Credit Holdings LLC as the lending counterparty. Liquidity cushions were thin.
