|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2020 | ~$75M | n/d | n/d | Pre-rebrand |
| FY2021 | ~$73M | n/d | n/d | COVID disruption |
| FY2022 | ~$95M | n/d | n/d | Revenue peak |
| FY2023 | ~$77M | ~16%* | n/d | Supply-chain drag |
| FY2024 | $91.2M | 16% | ($0.5M) | Straddles Ch.11; incl. $32.5M reorg. gain |
| FY2025 | $85.6M | 27% | $7.9M | First positive full-year EBITDA |

*Nine-month figure through December 2022. Full-year margin not separately disclosed pre-filing. Sources: [Capstone Green Energy Q3 FY2023 press release](https://www.capstoneenergyplus.com/news/press-releases/detail/3994/); [Capstone Green Energy FY2025 annual results](https://www.capstoneenergyplus.com/news/press-releases/detail/4040/).

## The Filing

Jamison's August 14, 2023 resignation (detailed in Leadership chapter) preceded the September 28, 2023 Chapter 11 filing by thirty-six days. The filing was accompanied by a Transaction Support Agreement executed the same day with Broad Street Credit Holdings LLC and Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group in their respective capacities as consenting lender and collateral agent. Capstone simultaneously disclosed $3.0 million of new-money bridge financing provided one week earlier, on September 22, with a committed $12.0 million debtor-in-possession facility available upon court approval — total DIP support of $15.0 million.

Pre-petition debt of $56.0 million was haircut to $25.0 million. Existing common stockholders preserved roughly 62.5 percent equity participation — materially more equity-preserving than typical contested Chapter 11 outcomes — with Goldman Sachs taking the remaining 37.5 percent stake. At emergence, total post-emergence funded debt stood at $25.0 million.

## Reporting Gaps and the FY2024 Transition Year

The move to OTCQX reporting cadence imposed a materially reduced disclosure rhythm relative to the NASDAQ-listed predecessor. The fiscal-2024 10-K, covering the twelve months ended March 31, 2024 — a period that straddled the Chapter 11 filing, the DIP process, and the emergence — was filed late, in autumn 2024. CFO Juric described it as "a pivotal milestone in our path toward full compliance with SEC reporting requirements." No revenue or operating-metric figures appeared in the accompanying press release; investors had to navigate the underlying 10-K directly for financial detail. Full-year fiscal-2024 revenue, which emerged in the fiscal-2025 comparatives, stood at $91.2 million, a figure that blended the final pre-filing quarters with the post-emergence operating period and was inflated by a $32.5 million reorganisation gain that generated $7.4 million of statutory net income against an underlying adjusted EBITDA of negative $0.5 million.

## The First Positive EBITDA

The fiscal-2025 results delivered the milestone that had defined a generation of Capstone management aspirations. Full-year revenue of $85.6 million fell modestly from the prior year's $91.2 million, but gross margin expanded to 27 percent from 16 percent, operating cash flow turned positive at $7.7 million, and adjusted EBITDA reached $7.9 million. Canino did not understate the significance:

> "In all of its 37-year history, the Company has never delivered positive Adjusted EBITDA over a full fiscal year."

He added: "We have changed the culture and truly changed the landscape of what Capstone's true potential is."

On the balance sheet, cash on hand grew to $8.7 million from $2.1 million a year earlier — a swing that provided the first credible liquidity buffer of the post-emergence period. The previously disclosed SEC investigation, which had added regulatory uncertainty through 2024, was closed with no action taken.

## Data-Centre Positioning

In October 2025, Capstone announced an 800-volt direct-current microturbine engineered with Microgrids 4 AI, Inc. for NVIDIA Kyber and Rubin Ultra rack platforms. Canino framed the rationale: "Our 800 VDC microturbine is designed for this new reality, building clean, reliable, redundant and direct high-voltage DC power." No contract volumes or revenue guidance specific to the data-centre channel had appeared in filings through May 23, 2026.

---

**Disclosure note:** Capstone Energy+ (CGEH) reports on an OTCQX cadence with materially reduced frequency and depth relative to its former NASDAQ-listed status. Quarterly earnings releases are published without associated analyst calls; the SEC investigation disclosure and the late filing of the FY2024 10-K both underscore the reduced transparency of the post-emergence reporting environment. Investors should treat the FY2024 revenue figure — which straddles the restructuring — and the accompanying net income as structurally non-comparable to pre- or post-filing periods.

chapters.title: Post-emergence executive team and the restructured-equity board
chapters.body:
## A Sixteen-Year Tenure Ends in Crisis

For the better part of two decades, Darren Jamison defined the Capstone Turbine identity. Appointed chief executive in 2007, Jamison presided over the company's expansion from a niche aerospace-derived turbine manufacturer into a global distributed-power platform — navigating the Capstone Green Energy rebrand in 2021 and building a distribution network spanning eighty-eight countries. By the time the company's financial position had deteriorated to the point of prepackaged bankruptcy, Jamison had logged roughly sixteen years in the chief executive role, an unusually long tenure for a small-cap industrials company. On August 14, 2023, Capstone Green Energy [announced his departure](https://www.capstonegreenenergy.com/news/press-releases/detail/4012/), effective August 22 — five weeks before the Chapter 11 filing in the District of Delaware. The board offered no strategic rationale for the separation beyond a standard statement of thanks for his years of service. [Turbomachinery Magazine](https://www.turbomachinerymag.com/view/ceo-resignation-leaves-vacancy-at-capstone-green-energy) noted at the time that the resignation left a leadership vacancy at a precarious moment.

## Flexon as Stabilising Force

Into the vacuum stepped Robert C. Flexon. A director since 2017 and board chair since 2021, Flexon was a credible operator: he had run Dynegy Inc. through its own bankruptcy restructuring and subsequent $3.3 billion sale to Vistra Energy, establishing a reputation as a utility-sector turnaround executive. On August 9, 2023, the board elevated him to Executive Chairman and, from the effective date of Jamison's resignation, to Interim President and Chief Executive Officer — a dual mandate that made him the company's de facto leader through the Chapter 11 process.

Flexon guided Capstone through the prepackaged reorganisation without meaningful operational disruption. Goldman Sachs's credit facility converted into preferred equity in Capstone Green Energy LLC, giving it a 62.5% controlling economic interest. Flexon: "With Chapter 11 behind us and a much stronger financial position, we can now fully focus on our distribution partners."

The five-person board assembled at emergence reflected the new ownership realities. Alongside Flexon as Chairman, the [December 2023 announcement](https://www.capstoneenergyplus.com/news/press-releases/detail/4019/) named Denise M. Wilson as Lead Independent Director, and three additional directors: Yon Yoon Jorden, technology entrepreneur Ping Fu, and Robert F. Powelson. Wilson brought utility-sector operating credibility — she had served as Executive Vice President and President of Alternative Energy Businesses at NRG Energy from 2011 to 2016. Ping Fu, co-founder and former chief executive of 3D imaging software company Geomagic (acquired by 3D Systems in 2013), provided technology and entrepreneurship experience and also held a seat on the Live Nation Entertainment board. Powelson arrived with a distinctive regulatory pedigree: a former Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission chairman who served as a Federal Energy Regulatory Commissioner from 2017 to 2018, he had subsequently become President and Chief Executive of the National Association of Water Companies. His presence gave the post-emergence board a credible regulatory interface for an energy company navigating utility interconnect and distributed-generation permitting environments.

**Board composition at December 2023 emergence**

| Director | Role | Prior Relevant Background |
|---|---|---|
| Robert C. Flexon | Chairman & Interim CEO | Dynegy CEO; utility restructuring |
| Denise M. Wilson | Lead Independent Director | NRG Energy EVP; alternative energy |
| Yon Yoon Jorden | Director | Serial CFO; AdvancePCS, WellPoint |
| Ping Fu | Director | Geomagic founder/CEO; 3D Systems CSO |
| Robert F. Powelson | Director | FERC Commissioner; PA PUC Chairman |

Notably absent from the emergence board was any named representative of Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group or its affiliated entities, despite Goldman's preferred equity stake representing the dominant economic interest in the operating subsidiary. The Goldman position was structured at the subsidiary level rather than as direct common equity in the listed holding company; the OTCQX-listed CGEH held a minority residual claim on the economics until the restructuring was completed. This structural layering meant the Goldman economic interest was reflected in the capital structure rather than directly in boardroom representation — a governance arrangement that would generate friction in subsequent periods.

## The Canino Appointment

The permanent chief executive search concluded on March 11, 2024. [Capstone announced](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240312283880/en/Capstone-Green-Energy-Announces-Vince-Canino-as-its-President-and-Chief-Executive-Officer) the appointment of Vincent J. Canino as President and Chief Executive Officer and a member of the board, with an annual base salary approved by the Compensation and Human Capital Committee of $550,000. Flexon simultaneously transitioned from Executive Chairman to Non-Executive Chairman, a role he assumed April 1, 2024.

Canino's background (summarised in Snapshot) includes eight years leading Smardt Chiller Group and COO tenure at ESS Inc. (NYSE: GWH) through March 2024, giving him direct exposure to energy storage and microgrid financing.

Also in February 2024, the board added John P. Miller as an independent director. Miller brought more than forty years of executive management across manufacturing, distribution, and transportation, including a stint as Chief Executive Officer of Power Solutions International, Inc. from 2017 to 2021 and senior vice-president roles at Navistar International. His appointment added both audit-committee depth and industrial-manufacturing operational experience.

## CFO Evolution

John J. Juric had been in place as Chief Financial Officer since March 6, 2023 — appointed in the final months before the Chapter 11 filing and carrying the company through the restructuring process. Juric brought more than twenty-five years of finance and manufacturing experience, having previously served as CFO of USALCO, a water-treatment chemistry provider, and in divisional CFO roles at Fiberweb. He remained CFO through the emergence, through the Canino appointment, and through the subsequent operating rebuild — until, on November 1, 2025, he resigned without stated cause. The simultaneous announcement on November 5, 2025 of Juric's departure and the subsequent governance events drew immediate investor attention.

Miller, who had served on the board's Audit Committee as its chair, was appointed Interim Chief Financial Officer effective November 2, 2025, assuming dual board and executive roles. No permanent CFO had been named as of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, leaving the finance function under interim leadership during a period of significant capital activity.

## A Board Fracture and Reset

The CFO departure was not the lead item in the November 2025 announcement. On October 30, 2025, Robert Flexon had resigned from the board entirely — the first clean break with the company he had steered through bankruptcy. The cited reason was blunt: a [disagreement over the company's strategic direction](https://www.tradingview.com/news/tradingview:020240f4f5f31:0-capstone-green-energy-announces-board-and-cfo-changes/), with Flexon having expressed concern about any alternative that diluted common stockholders without addressing the company's debt profile. The subtext was the board's active evaluation of capital-raise structures that would use preferred equity or convertible instruments to retire the legacy Goldman Sachs position — precisely the transaction that would close four months later. Robert Powelson was appointed Interim Chairman of the Board effective October 31, 2025.

Two further independent directors had by then joined the board. Christopher J. Close was appointed effective June 16, 2025, bringing the board to seven members. Close, then 59, had more than thirty-five years of senior financial leadership — CFO tenures at Noramco and Preferred Sands, earlier career finance roles at Exelon, Constellation Energy, and Airgas, and PricewaterhouseCoopers audit experience at the start of his career. He was appointed to chair the Audit Committee. At the August 12, 2025 virtual annual meeting of stockholders, Robert F. Beard was elected as a Class I director, bringing the board to eight members. Beard had retired as Chief Operating Officer of UGI Corporation and Chief Executive Officer of UGI Utilities, where he had directed a $1.3 billion midstream acquisition and led multi-billion-dollar capital programmes; he subsequently served on the Black Hills Corporation board. His addition aligned with Capstone's push to deepen midstream and utility relationships.

After Flexon's October departure the board stood at seven. The Monarch investment closing (detailed in Snapshot) redeemed Goldman Sachs's preferred position and granted Monarch two board seats on a seven-member board — appointments that remained undisclosed as of May 23, 2026.

## Disclosure Gaps

Several governance questions remain inadequately documented in Capstone Energy+'s public disclosures as of the snapshot date. Yon Yoon Jorden, who joined the board at the December 2023 emergence, no longer appeared on the company's IR management-team page; the timing and circumstances of her departure from the board were not the subject of any press release or 8-K filing traceable through the company's investor relations archive, leaving a gap in the governance record. The identity of any Monarch-appointed directors — given Monarch's contractual right to two seats on the seven-member board — had not been disclosed. And the permanent CFO search, presumably underway since November 2025, had not produced a public announcement. For a listed company with ambitions of graduating to a national securities exchange within twelve months of the March 2026 capital raise, those disclosure gaps are material: institutional investors accustomed to NYSE or NASDAQ governance standards will expect a permanent CFO, a fully disclosed director roster, and explicit committee assignment disclosure for any new board members before the listing application is credibly advanced.

---
*Sources: [Capstone Energy+ IR — management team](https://ir.capstoneenergyplus.com/management-team) · [Capstone Energy+ IR — board of directors](https://ir.capstoneenergyplus.com/board-of-directors) · [CEO transition press release, August 2023](https://www.capstonegreenenergy.com/news/press-releases/detail/4012/) · [Chapter 11 emergence press release, December 2023](https://www.capstoneenergyplus.com/news/press-releases/detail/4019/) · [Vince Canino appointment, March 2024](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240312283880/en/Capstone-Green-Energy-Announces-Vince-Canino-as-its-President-and-Chief-Executive-Officer) · [Christopher Close appointment, June 2025](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250623106595/en/Capstone-Green-Energy-Appoints-Christopher-Close-to-Its-Board-of-Directors) · [Board and CFO changes, November 2025](https://www.tradingview.com/news/tradingview:020240f4f5f31:0-capstone-green-energy-announces-board-and-cfo-changes/) · [Monarch investment announcement, March 2026](https://www.capstonegreenenergy.com/news/press-releases/detail/4065/) · [Monarch investment closing, March 2026](https://ir.capstoneenergyplus.com/press-releases/detail/4066)*

chapters.title: Oil-and-gas, industrial CHP, district energy, AI data centres, and the microturbine supply chain
chapters.body:
## Oil and Gas: The Anchor Segment

Throughout most of Capstone Turbine Corporation's publicly traded history, the oil and gas vertical was the company's largest revenue contributor, accounting for roughly 40 to 60 percent of annual product revenues in the years immediately preceding the Chapter 11 filing, according to the company's annual reports filed with the SEC during its NYSE listing period. The application that drove that concentration was deceptively straightforward: microturbines convert associated gas — the methane-rich byproduct that emerges at the wellhead alongside crude oil — into on-site electricity, eliminating flaring, reducing emissions, and powering pumps, compressors, and communications equipment at remote well pads where grid interconnection is economically impractical or physically unavailable.

The C200S and packaged C600S/C1000S configurations became the workhorses of this segment, tolerating lean maintenance schedules at unmanned upstream sites. Capstone's public filings identified the Permian Basin, the Eagle Ford, and broader Appalachian shale plays as geographies where the installed base was concentrated in North America. Internationally, the company had material exposure to Russian upstream operators through a distributor relationship; that channel was severely disrupted following the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine and the subsequent rounds of Western export controls, and Capstone Green Energy's annual reports for fiscal years 2022 and 2023 explicitly cited Russia-related revenue deterioration as a material headwind. Specific named upstream customers have not been disclosed in any OTCQX filing reviewed within the frozen window; this is a persistent disclosure gap that reflects both the OTCQX reporting framework and Capstone's historic practice of aggregating customer data by vertical rather than by name.

Post-emergence under Capstone Energy+, the company has continued to emphasise the oil and gas segment in IR communications as a source of recurring service revenue from the installed base, even as new unit shipments to the segment remain constrained by the company's post-restructuring manufacturing capacity and working capital position. The installed base represents a service annuity — long-term parts and maintenance agreements, renewal of Factory Protection Plan contracts — that is structurally more durable than new-unit revenue during a capital-constrained period.

## Industrial Cogeneration: The CHP Installed Base

Combined heat and power installations constitute the second major customer pillar. Exhaust heat at roughly 260°C is routed to heat recovery units for hot water, steam, or absorption cooling — achieving system efficiencies of 70–80 percent (as detailed in Business Segments).

Capstone's industrial CHP customer base has historically encompassed food and beverage processing, pharmaceuticals, light manufacturing, and commercial greenhouse operations. As with the oil and gas segment, the company's public disclosures have consistently withheld specific customer names at the individual account level; filings reference customer categories and geographies rather than named counterparties. The California market, given the state's elevated electricity rates and regulatory support for distributed generation under SGIP (the Self-Generation Incentive Program), has been a persistent concentration point. Pre-bankruptcy, Capstone's 10-K filings routinely flagged that a small number of large distributor accounts — rather than end-users directly — represented a meaningful share of product revenue, meaning the company's direct visibility into the end-customer mix was itself partially mediated by the distributor channel.

Post-emergence, the shift toward Energy-as-a-Service contracting — in which Capstone Energy+ retains ownership of the generation asset and sells electrons and thermal output under a long-term offtake agreement rather than selling the hardware outright — is intended to deepen direct relationships with industrial end-users. The EaaS model improves customer stickiness and creates a recurring revenue stream, but it also requires Capstone Energy+ to carry the capital cost of the installed asset on its own balance sheet, placing demands on the post-restructuring capital structure that remain a watch item for investors.

## District Energy: Campuses, Hospitals, and Contract Longevity

University campuses and hospital complexes represent the district energy segment of Capstone's customer base. The appeal is structural: a large campus has sustained thermal and electrical loads around the clock, a long-term planning horizon that matches the economics of CHP investment, and often an explicit sustainability mandate from trustees or accreditation bodies. Hospitals add the critical requirement for resilience — uninterruptible on-site generation that can island from the grid during outages, a requirement that Capstone's microturbines satisfy in part because their fast-start capability (reaching full output in roughly 60 seconds from cold) enables them to serve as both primary generation and backup within a single asset.

The district energy segment is where Capstone's multi-unit packaged systems — combining four to six C200S units, or multiple C1000S units, in a single containerised enclosure — have found natural application. Capstone has referenced university and hospital campus deployments in general terms in IR materials but, consistent with the broader disclosure pattern, has not published a named-customer list in OTCQX-period filings reviewed within the frozen window.

## AI Data Centres: The Post-Emergence Growth Narrative

Capstone Energy+ has explicitly targeted AI data centre operators as a new customer category, leveraging the utility interconnect queue times stretching three to seven years in key markets. Data centre operators value the oil-free design (minimising technician visits), fast-start capability, and low vibration profile. As of May 23, 2026, no publicly named AI data centre customer had been announced — the pipeline remains directional rather than contractual.

## The Microturbine Supply Chain

Capstone Energy+'s manufacturing footprint is concentrated at its Southern California campus, historically in Chatsworth and subsequently in Van Nuys. The company has long described a substantially vertically integrated manufacturing model for its core rotating and thermal components, which it has argued is necessary to protect proprietary tolerances in the air-bearing assembly and the recuperator.

| Component | Description | Capstone's approach |
|---|---|---|
| Air bearings | Foil-type hydrodynamic bearings; no oil lubrication; single-shaft assembly | Manufactured in-house; core IP |
| Recuperator heat exchanger | Primary surface, counterflow design; stainless steel foil construction; recovers ~75% of exhaust enthalpy | Manufactured in-house; historically a supply bottleneck at volume ramp |
| Combustor | Low-NOx lean-premixed design; natural gas, propane, associated gas, biogas, hydrogen-blend capable | In-house; combustor design is fuel-flexibility-critical |
| Power electronics / inverter | High-speed generator output rectified and inverted to grid-synchronous AC; digital control board | Partially in-house, with contract manufacturing for electronics sub-assemblies |
| Enclosure and balance-of-plant | Containerised packaging, heat recovery ducting, controls integration | Mix of in-house fabrication and outside suppliers |

The recuperator is the component that has historically created the most operational risk in Capstone's supply chain. Because the recuperator operates continuously at high temperatures and differential pressures, fatigue cracking over a multi-year operating cycle requires scheduled replacement; managing recuperator lead times and inventory has been a recurring operational challenge flagged in pre-bankruptcy filings. Post-emergence, the company has not provided granular supply chain disclosures in OTCQX-period communications, leaving the current state of recuperator inventory and supplier relationships opaque.

## Fuel Flexibility Advantages

Capstone's fuel flexibility (detailed in Business Segments) is operationally significant across all customer segments. For AI data centres, pipeline natural gas positions the microturbine as lower-emission than diesel backup and dispatchable in ways solar-plus-storage cannot replicate across multi-day weather events — the most technically defensible element of the bridge-power pitch.

chapters.title: Where Capstone Energy+ sits against Bloom Energy, Cummins, Caterpillar, and broader distributed power
chapters.body:
## A Crowded Arena with Fragmented Technology Stacks

Distributed power generation is not a single market but a collection of overlapping niches separated by scale, fuel type, emissions tolerance, and deployment context. Capstone Energy+'s competitive position as of the spring 2026 snapshot was shaped by three structural realities: its microturbine technology occupied a narrow band of the power density spectrum where its engineering characteristics genuinely differentiated it from alternatives; the dominant installed base of distributed backup and prime power worldwide remained reciprocating engine gensets supplied at scale by Cummins, Caterpillar, and a long tail of regional assemblers; and Bloom Energy had moved aggressively into the same premium, low-emissions distributed-power segment that Capstone historically occupied, with substantially more capital, a larger installed base, and a NYSE listing that afforded it investor visibility and financing flexibility that Capstone — a small-cap OTCQX-listed post-bankruptcy company — could not match.

## The Genset Floor: Cummins and Caterpillar

Reciprocating engine gensets from Cummins (CMI) and Caterpillar (CAT) established the de facto price floor for distributed backup and prime power. Diesel and natural gas gensets from both companies could be procured for installed costs typically in the range of $300 to $600 per kilowatt at commercial and industrial scales — materially below the $1,000 to $2,000-plus per kilowatt range that industry practitioners associated with microturbine installations. That capex gap was the persistent headwind against which every microturbine vendor, including Capstone, competed. Cummins's Power Generation segment and Caterpillar's Electric Power division collectively represented a multi-billion-dollar global franchise with deep distribution networks, standardised service infrastructure, and decades of customer familiarity. Caterpillar's Solar Turbines subsidiary also competed in small industrial gas turbines at larger scales — generally above 1 MW and extending into multi-megawatt packages — a range where Capstone's C1200S and packaged multi-unit systems touched the lower edge.

The reciprocating engine's disadvantages were well-documented in distributed-generation literature. NOx emissions from natural gas reciprocating engines, absent selective catalytic reduction aftertreatment, ranged from roughly 50 to several hundred parts per million — an order of magnitude above the sub-9 ppm NOx specification Capstone claimed for its C200S and larger units under natural gas firing. In air quality non-attainment areas — the South Coast Air Quality Management District in Southern California being the most commercially significant — that emissions gap translated directly into permitting constraints that disadvantaged genset alternatives. Maintenance intervals for reciprocating engines, driven by oil and filter change cycles, typically fell between 500 and 2,000 hours; Capstone cited scheduled maintenance intervals of 8,000 hours for its units, a function of the air-bearing rotor design that eliminated liquid lubrication. Neither the emissions advantage nor the maintenance interval claim could be independently verified from Capstone's OTCQX-level public filings as of the snapshot date — the company's post-emergence financial disclosures did not publish independent benchmarking data on a comparable basis.

Generac (GNRC), primarily a residential and light-commercial backup power vendor, occupied a lower scale range and did not represent a direct competitive threat in the industrial, oil-and-gas, or data-centre segments that Capstone pursued.

## Bloom Energy: The Premium-Segment Rival

The most pointed competitive comparison for a sophisticated distributed-power investor was with Bloom Energy (BE), the San Jose-based solid-oxide fuel cell manufacturer. Where Capstone competed on microturbine technology, Bloom deployed electrochemical energy conversion — solid-oxide fuel cells that consumed natural gas or hydrogen to produce electricity at roughly 53–65 percent electrical efficiency in fuel cell mode, materially above the 25–30 percent simple-cycle electrical efficiency of Capstone's microturbines. Bloom's Energy Servers, packaged in modular 100-kilowatt increments and typically deployed in multi-hundred-kilowatt to multi-megawatt configurations, had accumulated a substantial commercial and enterprise installed base across technology campuses, hospitals, retail chains, and, by the early 2020s, data centre operators including several hyperscalers.

Bloom's strategic pivot toward AI data centre power was explicit and well-capitalised. The company's fiscal 2024 revenues exceeded $1.3 billion, its NYSE listing gave it equity currency for growth capital, and its partnerships with hyperscaler operators were disclosed in SEC filings. Capstone's post-emergence revenue scale — not fully disclosed in accessible OTCQX filings as of the snapshot date — was categorically smaller; the disclosure gap here is material and should not be papered over. Bloom operated in a different financial weight class.

The technology comparison was not simply an efficiency table. Bloom's SOFC units required natural gas infrastructure or hydrogen supply and did not offer the same tolerance for degraded-quality or variable-composition fuel streams that made Capstone microturbines commercially interesting in oil-and-gas flare-gas recovery. Capstone's fuel flexibility — documented across natural gas, propane, liquefied petroleum gas, flare or associated gas, biogas, digester gas, and hydrogen blends — was a specific engineering characteristic that SOFC technology replicated less cleanly at the lower-quality end of the fuel spectrum. In oil and gas upstream applications where associated gas composition could vary substantially by field, the microturbine's tolerance for fuel variability was a genuine differentiator.

## Japanese and International Microturbine Alternatives

Within the narrower microturbine sub-segment, Capstone's competitive set was thin. Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Kawasaki Heavy Industries, and IHI Corporation each maintained small gas turbine and microturbine programs, but their commercial focus in distributed generation sat at larger scales and served primarily domestic Japanese industrial and utility markets. No Japanese vendor had established a material competing commercial footprint against Capstone in North America or the oil-and-gas-facing international markets that historically comprised Capstone's distribution network. European microturbine vendors, including earlier-stage development-stage companies, had not achieved the installed base or product range breadth that Capstone had accumulated over three decades. As of the snapshot date, Capstone appeared to retain meaningful position as the largest volume commercial microturbine manufacturer in the Western Hemisphere, though that position reflected a thin competitive field rather than a robust moat.

## The EaaS Contracting Layer

Capstone's post-emergence strategic communications emphasised the Energy-as-a-Service model as a competitive differentiator distinct from its technology characteristics. The EaaS structure — in which Capstone or its distribution partners retained equipment ownership and charged customers on a per-kilowatt-hour or service-fee basis — reduced customer upfront capital commitment and shifted the capex gap relative to genset alternatives into an operating-cost comparison. Bloom Energy had long operated a similar model through its Power Purchase Agreement and managed-services offerings; Cummins and Caterpillar sold equipment through dealers and did not historically operate at-scale EaaS structures comparable to fuel cell or microturbine vendors.

Whether Capstone's EaaS pipeline had converted into a durable recurring revenue base by the snapshot date could not be determined from available public disclosures. OTCQX reporting requirements are materially less demanding than those governing NASDAQ or NYSE-listed companies; Capstone's CGEH filings did not disclose contracted EaaS backlog, customer concentration, or revenue composition with the granularity available from Bloom's 10-K filings.

## The Data Centre Positioning Problem

| Vendor | Technology | Typical installed cost/kW | NOx emissions | Fuel flexibility | Data centre deployment evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cummins / CAT gensets | Reciprocating engine | ~$300–$600 | High (50–500+ ppm) | Diesel, nat gas | Widespread (standard backup) |
| Bloom Energy | Solid-oxide fuel cell | ~$5,000–$8,000+ | Very low | Nat gas, H₂ | Disclosed hyperscaler partnerships |
| Capstone Energy+ | Microturbine | ~$1,000–$2,000+ | Ultra-low (<9 ppm) | Broad fuel range | Cited as target; no disclosed deployments as of snapshot |

The AI data centre bridge-power opportunity created a specific competitive intersection. Hyperscaler operators facing utility interconnect queue delays of five to ten years in constrained markets needed dispatchable on-site generation that could be deployed in weeks rather than years. Diesel gensets remained the default solution — fast to source, widely available, financeable — but faced NOx and particulate emissions constraints that complicated air permitting in California, the Pacific Northwest, and Northern Virginia data centre corridors. Microturbines' emissions profile was therefore a structural advantage in those specific geographies. Capstone's management communications highlighted this positioning explicitly in post-emergence investor materials.

The competitive risk was straightforward: Bloom Energy was better-capitalised, had existing data centre customer relationships, and operated at power densities more suited to the multi-megawatt blocks that hyperscalers typically specified. Capstone's C1200S and packaged multi-unit systems could aggregate to several megawatts, but the project execution capability of a post-bankruptcy small-cap company competing for hyperscaler contracts alongside Bloom's commercial organisation represented an execution gap that public disclosures did not resolve. As of the snapshot date, no Capstone Energy+ data centre deployment had been publicly disclosed with the specificity — customer name, power capacity, contract structure — that would allow an investor to assess whether the strategic positioning had translated into commercial traction.

chapters.title: From 2000 IPO through Capstone Green Energy rebrand, Chapter 11, and AI data centre opportunity
chapters.body:
## Catalyst Framework

The Capstone Energy+ investment thesis hinges on three near-term catalysts whose resolution will determine whether the post-Chapter-11 positioning translates into sustained operating performance.

**Catalyst 1: AI Data Centre Contract Announcements**

The AI data centre bridge-power opportunity represents the primary growth vector in post-emergence communications. The underlying driver — utility interconnect queues stretching eighteen months to several years in major US markets — is well-documented. Capstone's C1000S and C1200S units, parallelable to double-digit megawatt deployments, can be commissioned on a fraction of the lead time required for permanent utility interconnection. The EaaS contracting structure developed since 2021 is well-suited to data centre operators with constrained capital budgets during construction.

As of May 23, 2026, pipeline commentary remained directional rather than contractual. No named data centre customer, contract volume, or revenue guidance specific to this channel had been disclosed. The pace of contract announcements will be the first test of commercial traction.

**Catalyst 2: Post-Emergence Revenue Trajectory**

Pre-Chapter-11 revenue ranged from $73 million (FY2021) to $95 million (FY2022), then retreated to $77 million (FY2023). The fiscal-2025 result of $85.6 million, paired with the first positive adjusted EBITDA of $7.9 million, established a baseline. Trailing twelve-month revenue through December 2025 approached $110 million. Whether this trajectory sustains — and whether the gross margin expansion to 27 percent proves durable — will determine whether restructured overhead translates to cash generation.

**Catalyst 3: National Exchange Listing**

The Monarch investment terms commit Capstone Energy+ to pursue a national exchange listing within twelve months of the March 2026 close. Migration from OTCQX to NASDAQ or NYSE would restore institutional accessibility, improve trading liquidity, and reinstate SEC reporting obligations that would close the disclosure gaps noted throughout this dossier. Execution on this timeline would represent the clearest signal of post-emergence normalisation.

chapters.title: Microturbine technology, air-bearing IP, and the EaaS platform
chapters.body:
## Air-Bearing Architecture as Core IP

The air-bearing architecture (described in Business Segments) remains the most defensible element of the technology platform. The design's maintenance paradigm — eliminating oil changes entirely — is especially valuable in remote or unmanned deployments.

The rotor assembly operates at approximately 96,000 revolutions per minute — far above the synchronous frequencies usable by the grid — meaning the turbine's raw AC output cannot be connected directly to utility infrastructure or building loads. Capstone's power electronics package, integrated into each turbine unit, first rectifies the high-frequency AC to DC and then inverts it to a clean 50 or 60 Hz output. This digital power electronics layer, often overlooked in assessments of the microturbine IP, is a significant barrier to replication: the control algorithms governing inverter switching, load tracking, and grid synchronisation represent decades of field-calibrated development.

## The Recuperator

The recuperator — a compact annular heat exchanger wrapped around the turbine core — raises electrical efficiency into the 25–33 percent range by recovering exhaust heat to pre-heat combustor inlet air. Combined with CHP operation, system efficiency reaches 70–80 percent (see Business Segments).

## Fuel Flexibility IP

The combustor's lean-premixed design operates at lower peak temperatures than conventional gas turbines, suppressing NOx formation and enabling operation on low-methane biogas, associated gas, and hydrogen blends. Hydrogen test data has been published, though precise commercial field blends remain undisclosed in OTCQX filings — an acknowledged disclosure gap for a strategically important optionality claim.

## The EaaS Software Layer

Energy-as-a-Service, as Capstone frames it, is not simply a financing structure. The company built a remote monitoring and fleet management platform — historically called the Capstone Remote Monitoring System — that aggregates real-time telemetry from deployed units into a centralised operations environment. Sensor data covering turbine inlet temperature, exhaust temperature, power output, fuel consumption, bearing air pressure, and dozens of additional parameters flow continuously from field units to Capstone's operations centre, enabling predictive maintenance interventions before faults develop into unplanned outages.

For a customer contracting under an EaaS arrangement — paying a fixed dollar-per-kWh or dollar-per-kWh-plus-thermal rate rather than purchasing hardware outright — the operational uptime guarantee that Capstone underwrites depends entirely on that monitoring infrastructure. The software layer is therefore not a value-added overlay but a load-bearing component of the EaaS business model. Capstone has described the monitoring system as proprietary, though granular disclosure on the underlying software architecture, API integrations with third-party SCADA or building management systems, or cybersecurity certification status was not available in public filings reviewed through the snapshot date.

## Patent Position and Portfolio Depth

Capstone's cumulative patent position spans several hundred issued patents across the United States and key international jurisdictions, accumulated over more than thirty years of microturbine development. The portfolio covers air-bearing design variants, recuperator geometries, combustor configurations, power electronics topologies, and control software methodologies. The age of the portfolio is itself a double-edged characteristic: issued patents on foundational air-bearing designs filed in the 1990s have largely expired, leaving those specific claim scopes in the public domain, while more recent filings on hydrogen-blend combustion, advanced recuperator materials, and EaaS software controls remain in-force and commercially relevant.

No competitor has successfully replicated the air-bearing microturbine design at commercial scale — Ingersoll Rand's discontinued PowerWorks product and Elliott Energy Systems' earlier turbine program both exited the market without establishing durable franchises — suggesting that the accumulated manufacturing know-how, field reliability data, and software calibration embedded in Capstone's platform constitutes a form of tacit IP that supplements the formal patent estate.

chapters.title: Post-Chapter-11 execution, AI demand conversion, competitive intensity, capital structure
chapters.body:
## Post-Chapter-11 Operational Execution

The most proximate risk: the OTCQX disclosure gap (detailed in Financial Deep Dive) means investors lack the quarterly visibility available for NASDAQ comparables. The Chapter 11 filing reflected operational scaling challenges and customer-receivable concerns — structural issues that balance-sheet restructuring alone does not resolve.

**Mitigants:** Core microturbine engineering and manufacturing remained intact; FY2025 delivered the first positive adjusted EBITDA. **Residual concern:** Without granular quarterly disclosure, the execution improvement thesis requires direct IR verification.

---

## AI Data Centre Opportunity Conversion

No specific AI data centre customer contract — customer identity, contracted capacity, revenue terms — had been disclosed through May 23, 2026. The category remains "emerging" in the company's own language.

**Mitigants:** Utility interconnect scarcity is real and documented; Capstone's configurations are technically suited. **Residual concern:** Technology suitability does not guarantee commercial conversion. Without disclosed contracts, AI data centre revenue cannot be modelled.

---

## Competitive Intensity

As detailed in Competitive Position, Capstone competes against well-capitalised incumbents: Bloom Energy (solid-oxide fuel cells, NASDAQ-listed, disclosed hyperscaler relationships), Cummins and Caterpillar (reciprocating gensets with global distribution and investment-grade balance sheets). Capstone's differentiators — air-bearing architecture, fuel flexibility, low emissions — have sustained commercial demand for three decades but have not translated into durable profitability. **Residual concern:** A small-cap OTCQX entity competing for hyperscaler contracts against investment-grade vendors faces structural disadvantages.

---

## Capital Structure Adequacy

The Monarch investment (March 2026) redeemed Goldman Sachs's preferred position and injected $112.5 million. Cash at FY2025 year-end stood at $8.7 million; post-Monarch balance sheet data was not public within the snapshot window. **Residual concern:** The pace at which EaaS deployments consume capital, and whether additional raises will be required, cannot be assessed given the disclosure gap.

---

## Customer Concentration

Capstone Turbine's pre-Chapter-11 revenue was historically concentrated in oil and gas and industrial CHP applications, with a material share routed through a small number of authorised distributors. Customer concentration — dependence on a limited number of end-users or channel partners — was a disclosed risk factor in pre-emergence SEC filings. Post-emergence, the concentration question persists: the shift toward EaaS contracting could reduce or increase concentration depending on whether EaaS contracts are signed with a diversified customer set or a handful of anchor counterparties. No post-emergence concentration disclosure was available through the snapshot date.

---

## Fuel Price Exposure

Capstone microturbines operate primarily on natural gas, with multi-fuel capability extending to propane, flare gas, and biogas. Revenue exposure to natural gas price volatility is indirect — Capstone sells and services equipment and does not typically take commodity price risk on the fuel itself. EaaS contract structures, however, where Capstone may retain responsibility for energy delivery economics, create potential pass-through exposure depending on contract terms. The EaaS model's economics are materially sensitive to the spread between gas input cost and the contracted energy delivery price. No EaaS contract terms had been disclosed publicly through the snapshot date, leaving fuel-price pass-through risk unquantified.

---

## Cross-Cutting: OTCQX Liquidity and Reporting Cadence

The migration from NASDAQ to OTCQX post-emergence is consequential across every risk category catalogued here. OTCQX-listed issuers are not subject to SEC periodic reporting obligations at the frequency or depth required of exchange-listed companies. Bid-ask spreads are typically wider than NASDAQ comparables; institutional participation is lower; and the secondary-market liquidity available to an investor seeking to exit a position may be materially constrained relative to what the pre-emergence listing offered. For a sophisticated investor evaluating Capstone Energy+ as a post-restructuring turnaround, the OTCQX structure means that the standard diligence toolkit — quarterly earnings, 10-K/10-Q SEC filings, earnings call transcripts, sell-side coverage — is partially or wholly unavailable. Each of the six risks above carries a higher residual uncertainty as a direct consequence of that reduced disclosure environment, and that structural feature should be treated as a standalone risk rather than merely a disclosure inconvenience.

chapters.title: AI data centre bridge-power scaling, EaaS conversion, and the 2026-2028 horizon
chapters.body:
## The Utility Interconnect Tailwind

The structural case for AI data centre bridge power — utility interconnect queues stretching five to seven years in major markets — is detailed in Business Segments and Customers & Supply Chain. As of late May 2026, the gap between Capstone's strategic narrative and verifiable commercial progress remained: no named data centre customer or specific pipeline figure had been disclosed.

## EaaS Conversion Path

EaaS creates near-term revenue headwinds — units deployed under long-term contracts don't generate immediate top-line recognition — while building the recurring revenue base that investors in distributed power platforms increasingly reward. FY2025's $14.4 million EaaS/rental contribution (17 percent of revenue) established a meaningful baseline. Tracking conversion progress requires direct IR engagement given OTCQX disclosure constraints.

## Legacy Verticals

Oil and gas and industrial CHP (detailed in Customers & Supply Chain) remain the core revenue base. Associated gas flaring restrictions continue tightening across US producing basins; CHP economics improved as commercial electricity prices rose post-pandemic. Whether improved economics translated to accelerated order activity is a question public disclosures do not answer.

## Risk Summary

Four risks dominate (detailed in Risks chapter): (1) competitive displacement from better-capitalised players, particularly Bloom Energy in data centre applications; (2) execution — translating FY2025's margin improvement into sustained cash generation; (3) OTCQX disclosure constraints; (4) capital requirements for EaaS deployment against a post-restructuring balance sheet.

## The Profitability Question

FY2025 delivered the first positive full-year adjusted EBITDA ($7.9 million) in the company's 37-year history. The post-Chapter-11 period offers conditions that had not previously coexisted: a structurally reduced cost base, an emerging AI data centre demand category, and an EaaS model building recurring revenue. Whether these conditions sustain profitability across the 2026-to-2028 window is the question the evidence cannot yet answer. The strategic logic is more compelling than at any prior point in the company's history; financial validation remains materially incomplete.

Revenue, margin, and balance-sheet data for fiscal years following the December 2023 emergence were not comprehensively available within the frozen window. Readers should consult OTCQX disclosure filings directly for current financial statements.

Packaged systems combine multiple microturbine units with inverter, energy storage, and control software to deliver multi-MW microgrid configurations for commercial, industrial, and data centre customers.

---

## Appendix D — Principal Customer Applications

Oil and gas (flared associated gas utilisation, upstream well-site power, midstream compression and processing); industrial cogeneration and combined heat and power; district energy serving university campuses, hospital complexes, and municipal systems; hotel and hospitality cogeneration; and the post-emergence strategic category of AI data centre backup-and-bridge power, serving operators facing utility interconnect queue delays across major U.S. and international markets.

## Appendix E — Competitive References

| Generac (GNRC, NYSE) | Standby and prime power generators; commercial and industrial |

Capstone's competitive differentiation rests on low-maintenance air-bearing microturbine architecture, multi-fuel flexibility, and the integrated EaaS contracting model rather than outright unit-cost parity with reciprocating alternatives.

---

## Appendix F — Primary Sources

OTCQX disclosures for ticker CGEH; Capstone Energy+ investor relations communications; Capstone Green Energy Holdings Chapter 11 filings, U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware (Case filed September 28, 2023); pre-emergence NASDAQ filings for Capstone Turbine Corporation and Capstone Green Energy Holdings; primary industry coverage via Bloomberg, Reuters, *The Wall Street Journal*, *Power Magazine*, and distributed-generation trade publications.

All research, financial data, corporate disclosures, and competitive references in this dossier reflect information available through **May 23, 2026**. Events, filings, financial results, and corporate developments occurring after that date are outside the scope of this document.
